name: Hassan Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying adult nursing. Three days a week are lectures and clinical skills in the simulation ward, where we practise on dummies, and I have my first placement block coming in the spring. At weekends I do bank shifts as a healthcare assistant at a nursing home called Maple Court, helping residents wash, eat and move around. I rent a room in a flat share with two other students. My dad is a warehouse supervisor and my mum is a school cook, and they chip in towards the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit overhyped, but some of it's useful. I'd tell friends that it'll help with paperwork, which nurses hate, and then life carries on. I wouldn't be shouting about it either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job looks pretty safe. People need nurses and carers, and no one has found a way around that. My only worry would be the usual one, which is pay not keeping up with prices and the health service being short of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing bank shifts, pay my rent, and use AI the odd time for a pharmacology explanation. I'd also put my first-year placement money aside. Nothing changes, so I'd just get on with learning the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, I think. I know it sounds dull, but I'm happy with dull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You do care-home shifts. What does AI look like from there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At Maple Court the nurses spend about a third of the shift on notes and forms. If a tool cut that down, that's time for the residents. Nurses at Maple Court spend a third of the shift on forms, so if a tool cuts that, it's more time for residents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make nursing a hard choice financially?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan, mostly. Nursing degrees are three years and the bursary is small. And you need a car for placements, which I don't have, so I'd have to find money for fuel or a bus pass.

say: I'd say AI is **overhyped**, but it could help nurses with paperwork.
I wouldn't be shouting about it either way.
think: My job looks **safe**, because no one has found a way around needing nurses.
My real worry is **pay** not keeping up with prices.
do: Keep the weekend **bank shifts** at the nursing home.
Use AI the odd time for **pharmacology** explanations.
S0.quote: Nurses at Maple Court spend a third of the shift on forms, so if a tool cuts that, it's more time for residents.
fieldNote: **Calm** because nursing demand feels secure, while pay and the loan remain his quiet worries.
Describes AI's use in terms of **forms**, drawn from his real shifts.
Balanced and **measured**, as his centre outlook suggests.

steps.text: Keep doing weekend bank shifts at Maple Court
Use the AI chatbot to explain pharmacology topics before exams
Put placement money aside for bus passes and fuel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good and bad, depending on how it's used. If it takes over the notes and the rota planning, that's great. If it's used to run a ward with fewer staff, it's not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel fine about my job. The writing, scheduling and checking tasks would change, and robots would only slowly reach the physical care. But I'd worry about the quality of care if management used software as a reason to cut hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the record-keeping tools at placement, since nurses will need them. I'd keep the bank shifts so I stay close to real patients, and I'd ask the sister at Maple Court how she sees it. I'd also spend a little more time on the clinical side, since that's what stays human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not about me, but about the staffing, because the care home is already stretched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in the nursing home would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking appointments, medication checks, care plans, the rota. The paperwork and scheduling would go to software, but washing a resident and noticing they're not themselves is still a person's job. That's what I'd focus on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you decide whether to try something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wait until someone I trust has used it for a few weeks. If a colleague says it works, I'll try it. That has served me okay so far, since I've not been burnt yet.

say: I'd say it's **good or bad** depending on how it is used.
I'd say software should not replace **staff** on the ward.
think: I feel **fine** about my job, since robots reach physical care slowly.
I worry managers will use software to cut **hours**.
do: Keep the bank shifts so I stay close to **patients**.
Ask the **sister** at Maple Court how she sees it.

fieldNote: His **own job** seems safe, and the unease is about staffing quality.
Waits until a **trusted colleague** has tested a tool, true to a steady profile.
Anchors on the **hands-on** side of care.

steps.text: Learn the electronic patient records tool during spring placement
Keep the weekend bank shifts at Maple Court
Ask the care home sister how her job might change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and we need the government to plan. I'd say hospitals and care homes need to keep human staff, and nobody should be dropped overnight. I'd say it calmly, because panicking helps no one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy. The thinking part of nursing, like notes and diagnosis support, would change in two years, and the physical part would be around 2031 with robots. I'd graduate in 2029, which gives me a couple of years, but I don't know what the job looks like after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the course, because nursing is the best bet I have. I'd save extra, since my parents' jobs in the warehouse and the school kitchen might change too. And I'd start learning the AI tools now, so I'm not the slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with some anxiety creeping in about my parents. Their jobs are exposed, and I'm the one who's meant to be getting a secure profession.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. Does nursing feel different from other jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nursing is more hands-on than most, so it should hold longer, maybe till the early 2030s. But two years gives me no time to adjust if I'm wrong. Nursing is hands-on so it should last longer, but two years leaves no time to adjust if I'm wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't panic, but let's talk about money. I'd ask my dad if the warehouse is using more automation already, and my mum if the school is changing its catering. I'd tell them I'll keep helping out where I can.

I'd say nobody should be **dropped overnight**.
think: The thinking side of nursing changes in **two years**, the physical side later.
My parents' warehouse and school kitchen jobs might change too, and that **worries** me.
do: Stay on the **course**, my best bet.
Save **extra** in case my parents' jobs change.
feel: **Uneasy**, with anxiety about my parents' jobs.
S2.quote: Nursing is hands-on so it should last longer, but two years leaves no time to adjust if I'm wrong.
fieldNote: His **own career** looks safer than most, but he thinks of his parents' exposure.
The **short window** is the problem, not nursing itself.
Pragmatic response: stay on course, **save** and learn tools.

steps.text: Stay on the nursing course and finish the first-year placement
Save an extra hundred a month from bank shifts
Use an AI tool every week to practise clinical notes
Sit down with my parents and go through their money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if the health service and government start now. I'd say nurses should help shape how the tools are brought in. I'd also say that every ward should keep a minimum number of people on shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel pretty okay. I'd graduate in 2029, have two years as a newly qualified nurse, and AGI would hit in 2031. Robots in 2034 are the bigger question for me, but I'd have a few years of experience by then to move into a specialist or supervising role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, get a ward job, and take extra training, like wound care or mental health. I'd learn the new tools as they arrive and save for a deposit. I'd also stay in the union, since nurses will need someone to speak up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, I think. A little uneasy, but five years feels like proper breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years you couldn't do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I could build experience and a specialty before the robots arrive. With five years I can get a specialty qualification before robots arrive, and that's something two years wouldn't allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the health service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want clear training on the tools, paid for and in work hours. And I'd want a promise that staffing levels will stay, written down, not just said in a press release.

I'd say nurses should help **shape** how the tools come in.

I'd aim for a **specialist** role before robots in 2034.
do: Finish the degree and take a **ward job**.
Do extra training in **wound care** or mental health.
feel: **Steady**, with a little unease and plenty of breathing room.
S3.quote: With five years I can get a specialty qualification before robots arrive, and that's something two years wouldn't allow.
fieldNote: The **timeline** lets him picture a specialist route.
Wants **written** staffing promises, not press releases.
Still **uneasy** about the robots in 2034, but far less than in the two-year world.

steps.text: Take a wound care course after qualifying
Learn each new ward software system as it arrives
Stay in the nurses' union and go to branch meetings
Save towards a flat deposit once I'm on a ward salary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and we should use it well. I'd tell friends not to stress, but to keep their skills fresh. And I'd say the health service needs to start planning properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be calm. I'd be a nurse for about six years before AGI and nine before robots, and I'd have a career and probably a family. It feels like something to keep an eye on rather than something to fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work as a nurse, and keep studying part-time toward a specialist qualification. I'd save for a house and keep learning tools as they arrive. And I'd stay flexible about where I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit proud that I picked a job people will still need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you stop worrying about with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop worrying about whether nursing is a safe bet. Ten years is enough to build a nursing career, buy a home and still have options if anything changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently with such a long time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably travel and work abroad for a year, since there'd be time. And I'd try a different setting, like community nursing, to see where I fit best.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** and we should use it well.
I'd tell friends to **keep skills fresh**.
think: I'd be a nurse for about **six years** before AGI and nine before robots.
It feels like something to **watch**, not fear.
do: Finish the degree and work as a **nurse**.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit proud of my choice.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to build a nursing career, buy a home and still have options if anything changes.
fieldNote: The **decade** removes his main worry and opens room for travel.
Pride in choosing work people will **need**, and a wish to try different settings.

steps.text: Qualify as a nurse and work on a ward for two years
Study part-time for a specialist nursing qualification
Save for a house deposit over the decade
Work abroad for a year once I'm qualified

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Nursing should last longer than most jobs, but I couldn't be sure, and my parents' jobs are more exposed than mine. What would help is clear staffing promises from the health service and paid training on the new tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not a big talker about the future, but I think about it more than I let on. It's nice to say it out loud to someone neutral.

headlineQuote: I'm not a big talker about the future, but I think about it more than I let on.
portrait: Hassan is a 19-year-old **adult nursing** student who works weekend bank shifts at a care home.
His dad is a warehouse supervisor and his mum a school cook, and their jobs worry him more than his own.
He is pragmatic and measured, uses AI now and then, and waits for a trusted colleague to try new tools.
He is calm when little changes and **uneasy** in the faster worlds, never alarmed.
He plans to stay on course, add a specialty and save, and wants staffing promises written down.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because there would be no time to adjust if he is wrong about nursing.
whatWouldHelp: Clear, written **staffing promises** from the health service.
Paid **training** on new tools during work hours.
